doc.title: Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes Interview, 1959-10-01

chapter: Paul Barnes: Last tour with King Oliver
title: Rejoining King Oliver in 1934 and the band lineup
summary: Oliver sends for Paul; he lists the band met in Paducah and says they came from all over, with little pay.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Yeah, he came down here and he pulled those boys and so they got me out the band for a while. And so they fought so much over the band, I just quit and I left the band to go. I quit the band. After I quit the band, the band just went down. So I joined the band with Walter Johnson. Had a fella they called Walter Johnson. So I joined with Walter Johnson's band and we did pretty good work around there. And we got the job at the American Legion that Gabriel had the job there for about ten years and we got the job from him at the American Legion. And everybody around there was crazy about Paul Bones' band. And when we left that just practically ruined Vincent Lopresto's place, you see, because the people stopped going there and they started coming over to the American Legion where we were playing. And that band just went on through. Well I stayed with Walter Johnson until 1934 and things wasn't so good. By that time King Oliver sent for me. And I was back again with King Oliver. Then, you understand? Well, 34 I went, I met them in Paducah, Kentucky. And, uh, let me see if I'll have the, yeah. I could give you the lineup of the men. We had, uh, I met them, we had a fella called Selma Payne. He was a saxophone player. And we had Buddy Harrell. He was a trumpet. We had a fella called Herman Elkins. He came from New York. He was a trumpet. He was the one that came all the way from New York with King. And this Herman Elkins, he was a trumpet player in the same band that Cab Calloway had taken over. And he was playing with them at that time. And we had a fella, uh, Leonard Phillips. He was playing trumpet. And King Oliver was playing trumpet. And trombone, we had a fella called Otto Jones. We called him Pete for shorts. And piano, a little short fella called Charlie Turan. And on drums we had Deebo Mills, Demit Mills. Deebo Demit Mills, that was a drum player. And bass we had Andrew, Dan Andrews on bass. The guitar was Bernie Cobb. And we had a director, Billy Coleman was a director. And a songster we had Doris Duff. That was a wonderful songster. That boy could sing. He didn't chant anyone when you hear him sing. I never forget that.
Where did most of those people come from? Any certain part of the country? They weren't from New Orleans, I guess. No, no.

They, they, the only New Orleans person in this, that I've just called was, excuse me, King Oliver and me. King Oliver. But they all come from all different parts of the country. Some from Kentucky and New York, you know. It's all over. Yeah, all different places. Well I was very happy to get into that band. It really sounded good. The band was good. But to my disappointment, the band, things were just bad. I didn't make any more. You want to stop that now? I'm running. Well you want, I didn't, I wasn't making any more with that band than I was with the other
little bands around home and down here.

Some nights we'd play with, you know, I'd come from all different parts of the country. Some of them come from all different parts of the country, some from Kentucky and New York, you know. Right in your book there from that time. Yeah. From that time. Yeah.

Yeah. I was just, I wasn't making any more with that band than I was with the other little bands around home and down here. Some nights we'd play, we'd make two dollars and maybe on the other nights we'd get a dollar sixty-eight cents a piece. That's what they, some nights, look, as much as, each is eighty-five cents a piece and it was just tough.
